taxonomy_teaching_note.caution: Flora of North America and many Texas fern references retain Cheilanthes/Pellaea, so the learner should not treat those familiar names as identification errors.

family_lesson.where_to_look_first: Ignore flowers entirely. Read the frond architecture, then flip a fertile frond over. In many local Pteridaceae the sori are marginal/submarginal and protected by the recurved leaf margin, creating a false indusium rather than a true indusium.
family_lesson.strongest_field_confirmation: Fern with divided fronds + sori near the blade/segment margin + no true indusium + margin often rolled over the sori as a false indusium. In local xeric members, leathery segments plus hairs/scales and rock-crevice habitat reinforce the ID.
core_characters: Ferns: no flowers, fruits or seeds; reproduction is by spores.
Rhizomes creeping to compact/erect and commonly scaly.
Fronds may be once to several times pinnate.
Stipe is the stalk below the leafy blade; rachis is its continuation through the blade.
Primary divisions are pinnae; divisions of pinnae are pinnules; the smallest divisions are ultimate segments.
Sporangia are commonly grouped in marginal or submarginal sori.
True indusia are absent in the family framework used here.
A recurved/revolute blade margin often protects the sori and functions as a false indusium/pseudo-indusium.
Hairs, scales, farina and rachis/stipe texture are often more diagnostic than overall green color.
Many local cheilanthoids are rock-crevice ferns adapted to seasonally dry, exposed sites.
avoid_overgeneralizing: Do not teach false indusia as present in every Pteridaceae species; the family is large and diverse.
Do not call every brown spot on a fern a sorus; first confirm regular placement and sporangia.
Do not call the false indusium a true indusium; it is rolled blade tissue, not a separate membrane.
Do not assume all ferns require wet shady forest; many Central Texas Pteridaceae occupy dry limestone/rock crevices.
Do not make drought-curling universal; it is a xeric adaptation seen strongly in some cheilanthoid ferns, not a required family character.
Do not treat older Cheilanthes/Pellaea names as wrong in field literature; current taxonomic treatments differ.

fern_parts_lesson.visual_rule: Always photograph one whole frond, one upper-surface close-up, one underside close-up, and the stipe/rhizome area when possible.

local_anchor_cards.look_here_first: Feel with your eyes, not your fingers: the frond surfaces look rough because of stiff basally swollen hairs. The small ultimate segments have inrolled margins and submarginal sori underneath.
confirms: Small tufted rock fern.
Dark red-purple to black stipe/rachis.
Frond generally twice divided toward the base.
Upper and lower surfaces roughened by distinctive stiff hairs.
Rachis/pinna axes with hairs and persistent scales.
Ultimate segments small, obtuse/ovate, with revolute margins.
Sori submarginal and appearing nearly continuous.
False indusium formed by the down-curved leaf margin.

fast_key: Fern with regular marginal/submarginal sori and rolled segment edge covering sori -> strongly supports Pteridaceae/cheilanthoid-cliffbrake framework.
Tiny rough hairy frond + scabrous ultimate segments -> source Cheilanthes horridula / current Hemionitis aspera.
Dark purple-black straight rachis + broad leathery segments + continuous marginal sori -> source Pellaea atropurpurea / H. atropurpurea.
Large fern with strongly zigzag/flexuous rachis -> source Pellaea ovata / H. ovata.
Dark rachis + narrow mucronate segments but no dramatic zigzag -> source Pellaea wrightiana / H. wrightiana.

definitions.indusium: A true separate flap/membrane covering a sorus.
definitions.false_indusium: The fern blade margin itself rolls/recurves over the sori and acts like a cover.

visual_sequence: label it FALSE INDUSIUM — blade tissue, not separate membrane
sori_and_indusia_lesson.family_caution: Kew explicitly notes that Pteridaceae lacks true indusia in this family-recognition framework, with marginal sori often protected by the in-rolled lamina margin.

drought_adaptation_lesson.key_point: Central Texas cheilanthoid/cliffbrake ferns are built for rock crevices and intermittent water, not permanently wet forest soil.
traits_to_show: dense hairs or scales in rough lipfern
rhizomes protected deep in rock cracks
fertile structures sheltered under rolled margins
drought_adaptation_lesson.behavior_caution: Some xeric ferns curl or contract their fronds/segments strongly during drought and reopen with moisture, but this should be presented as a xeric adaptation rather than a universal Pteridaceae ID character.
drought_adaptation_lesson.field_message: A curled brownish xeric fern may be drought-stressed rather than dead; check the rhizome and recent moisture before assuming mortality.

Aspleniaceae.tie_breaker: Typically has elongated sori along veins with a true linear indusium; Pteridaceae in this lesson has marginal/submarginal sori and no true indusium.

Dryopteridaceae.tie_breaker: Often has discrete round sori with a true round/reniform indusium; local Pteridaceae more often puts sori at or near the margin under recurved blade tissue.

Polypodiaceae.tie_breaker: Often has round naked sori away from the margin and fronds articulated to persistent stipe bases; the local Pteridaceae anchors show marginal bands/false indusia.

Dennstaedtiaceae.tie_breaker: Can also have marginal sori and false indusia, but commonly has an additional true indusium and long-creeping rhizomes; inspect soral construction rather than margin position alone.
